title: Placement: what electricity already does in your head
description: Ten short questions mark which later lessons to take slowly. Wrong answers do not lock you out.

blocks.md:
## No knobs yet

Ten short questions about a lamp, a battery, and a path. Wrong answers do not lock you out — they mark which later lessons to take slowly.

Pick the picture or the sentence that matches how a real loop behaves, not the story you wish were true. Later you will change a live circuit and see the lamp answer you.

```text
battery → resistor → lamp → battery
```

blocks.promptMd: Which picture can light a lamp?
blocks.explainMd: Charge needs a closed path out of the battery and back. An open gap is dark. A short skips the lamp and overheats the easy wire.

blocks.promptMd: In a series loop the current coming back to the battery is smaller because the lamp used it up.
blocks.explainMd: Current is the same all the way around one path. The lamp spends energy. The charge itself comes home.

blocks.promptMd: Voltage is best thought of as…

choices.md: A difference — a push between two points
A stuff that sits inside the wire
Something that only works with two different metals

blocks.explainMd: Voltage is a difference you measure across two points. It is not juice stored in copper, and it does not require two kinds of metal.

blocks.promptMd: If the push is 6 and the resistance is 3, what is the current? (I = V ÷ R)
blocks.explainMd: I = V ÷ R = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Resistance is not a brightness knob that ignores the relation.

blocks.promptMd: Two lamps share one path (series). The current through the second lamp is…

choices.md: The same as through the first
Less, because the first lamp used some up

blocks.explainMd: One path, one current. Series lamps share that current. They do not eat it on the way to the next lamp.

blocks.promptMd: Two lamps sit on two paths across the same battery (parallel). Each lamp sees…

choices.md: A dimmer share because the other lamp steals it

blocks.explainMd: Parallel branches see the same voltage. Currents split. A second lamp does not automatically steal the first lamp’s push.

blocks.promptMd: A thick extra wire skips the lamp and joins the battery ends. That is…

choices.md: A short — huge current and heat
More power, so a better circuit
The same as opening a switch

blocks.explainMd: A short is an easy extra path. Current soars, heat soars, and the lamp is often skipped. That is not a brighter win.

blocks.promptMd: Adding cells to a loop always makes the lamp brighter, no matter the resistance or the fuse.

choices.md: False — the loop and the limit still matter
True — more cells always means brighter

blocks.explainMd: More cells add push. Current is still push divided by squeeze, and a fuse can open. Extra cells are not a free brightness cheat.

blocks.promptMd: A circuit only works if the battery and the lamp are made of two different metals.
blocks.explainMd: You need a closed path and a difference (a push). Two different metals are a history story, not the rule.

blocks.promptMd: A fuse is optional decoration. You can skip it if you want the lamp as bright as possible.
blocks.explainMd: A fuse is a planned weak point. Skipping it so you can overshoot current is how wires melt. The limit is part of the win.
